P1 holds Kentucky, blocking the red monopoly. They might mortgage it rather than sell for $100.

Paying $185 for Illinois would fund p3's first yellow houses while leaving me unable to complete the red set.

Checking current board danger. p4's light blue properties with four houses each charge $450, $450, and $600. p1's Park Place at two houses is $500 and Boardwalk at three houses is $1400. Walking the trade would actually prevent p3 from building three yellow houses immediately. Paying $123 or more enables that construction.

Two houses on yellow properties are already possible without my help. Even distribution yields only moderate rent, so the immediate danger is not two houses versus three.

The $185 offer would only let p3 build one house on each yellow property, not two. That is not an immediate threat. The real danger is them eventually reaching two houses or hotels. I am now weighing whether Illinois is worth that price. I could complete the red set by adding Kentucky from p1, who has only $46 cash and may be forced to sell it if he cannot pay a rent.

Paying $185 for Illinois is a discount if the red set completes. The trade leaves me with only $213, which is insufficient to purchase Virginia Avenue and build even one house on the pink set.

P4 is the biggest threat. They have $484 cash and are close to completing an orange set, with light blue hotels incoming. Funding p3 would create a second dangerous player while I hold no monopoly. The $185 offer is well above the $122 ceiling, so I should reject it rather than counter higher.

p3 already rejected $120 and will not accept $122. Countering again would waste an exchange and signal I am still negotiating. I should reject firmly to preserve the option to trade later if their situation worsens. I have no properties to offer in a counter-trade, so rejecting is the only viable path. The public message should be firm without revealing my exact ceiling or that I am protecting Virginia cash.

A firm rejection message is being drafted to close the deal without insulting p3. I will not counter at $122 because that reveals my ceiling and invites a higher follow-up bid. If I reject, p3 might sell Illinois to p4 instead. p4 does not own red properties, so they could acquire it as a block against me and kill my red set entirely.

P4 has $484 and just bought Pennsylvania for $150. They might pay $185–200 for Illinois to block my red set. That would be worse than paying $185 myself. I still have the pink path via Virginia in the bank. The red set was a lottery anyway because p1 holds Kentucky. If p3 sells to p4 they will spend cash that could fund their own houses. P4 would not gain a complete set from Illinois.

P4 can afford both a light blue hotel and Illinois, so rejecting the trade does not prevent them from blocking my red set. I am now weighing whether to pay $185 anyway to secure a two-thirds red set and block p4. A completed red monopoly would be strong once Kentucky is acquired, since Indiana, Illinois, and Kentucky would charge excellent rent.

P1's cash is only $46, so he may go bankrupt before selling Kentucky. I am unsure whether a bankrupt player's properties return to the bank or are auctioned.

If p1 goes bankrupt to p4, p4 could acquire Kentucky and pair it with Illinois for a red monopoly. Owning Illinois myself would block that exact outcome. That insurance value is being weighed against the $185 cost.

The $123 threshold is the exact amount needed to build one house on each yellow property. The $185 offer would leave p3 with a $62 surplus after three houses, which is too little to build a fourth. The marginal damage of paying $185 is therefore exactly those three houses plus that leftover cash. Stopping the first yellow houses matters more than completing an unfinished red set, because a yellow monopoly becomes a cash engine that p3 can use to fund further construction.
